newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar falls to 18-month low on row.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar falls to 18-month low on row.

text.p: The Singapore dollar sank to an 18-month low against the U.S. dollar overnight after Malaysia said it was freezing new bilateral ties, dealers said on Thursday.
The local currency fell to a low of 1.4528/30, mainly on selling by European and New York funds when news of the row broke late on Wednesday.

Malaysia said it was freezing all official dealings, including granting of contracts to Singapore firms, over Singapore elder statesmen Lee Kuan Yew's jibe that Malaysia's Johor state was "notorious for shootings, car-jackings and muggings".
The Singapore dollar recovered in late morning trade on Thursday, partly on talk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).
The defacto central bank was said to have bought U.S. dollars near the highs of 1.4520/25. The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4475/85 at 0405 GMT against its opening 1.4520/25.
Local banks sold the U.S. dollar near its higher levels, triggering speculation of MAS intervention, but dealers were not immediately able to estimate the amount sold.
The MAS does not comment on forex interventions.
Dealers said the Singapore dollar was expected to hit the 1.4500 level in the medium term as it had been under pressure from fund flows into the higher-yielding Malaysian ringgit.
The Singapore dollar has depreciated some two percent against the US dollar since the start of the year.

"Basically, because of the row between Malaysia and Singapore, the market was quite nervous and the initial reaction in Europe was just to buy dollars against the Sing and the ringgit," said a U.S. bank dealer.
He said dollar/Sing looked well supported around 1.4460/80 but 1.4520 would pose a stiff barrier for the time being.

"The MAS exchange rate policy is to prevent extreme volatility caused by exactly this sort of knee-jerk reaction to unanticipated events," said Song Seng Wun, regional economist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett.
Dealers said much of the dollar buying on Thursday was driven by off-shore speculative funds.
"If the market does try 1.4525 later on and there's no confirmation of MAS (presence), then I think it will be higher. But I think 1.4500 is too high, too soon," said a Japanese bank dealer.
"I think the market's a little worried for sure. It seems the reasoning is that if this carries on, it'll do no good to Malaysia or Singapore," a U.S. bank dealer said.

"This just reflects the uncertainty about what would be the follow-up to the freezing of ties. It's going to be worse for Singapore than Malaysia in the context of impacts on the economy or earnings growth," said Song.
